input.quote: IBM reserves the right to investigate potential violations of the representations and warranties in Subsection 11.2(b).
input.rationale: On review, the AUDIT rule has no target in this agreement. There is no usage-, metering- or licence-compliance audit right binding Customer: no clause uses audit, inspect, verify, examine or records-access language against us; § 4.1/4.2 have IBM meter and invoice its own usage Charges without any right to audit our books; and § 12.1 grants a licence with no compliance-verification right. The only inspection-flavoured provision, § 11.3, is an abuse/acceptable-use enforcement right — IBM investigating suspected breaches of the content/AUP warranties in § 11.2(b) — which is a security and illegal-content mechanism, not a commercial audit, and § 11.3(a)/(b) plus p0137's emergency carve-out are the counterparts to that. Grafting audit-style limits (annual cap, 30 days' notice, 5% underpayment cost-shift, blanket no-systems-access) onto it would be directionally wrong in a hosting deal where IBM operates the environment: it would contradict p0137's emergency/legal-requirement notice standard and p0138's information obligation, bar IBM from responding to a second abuse or security incident, and import an inoperative payment trigger where no quantity is measured. I therefore withdraw the earlier insertion. The absence of any audit right against Customer is better than the playbook preferred position and favours us, so no redline is warranted; if a Service Option Attachment or Order Form later introduces usage verification, the AUDIT parameters should be applied there.
